main.title: Unification of Germany
main.summary: The German Empire was proclaimed on 18 January 1871 after the southern German states joined the Prussian-led federation.

cards.heading: Unification of Germany
cards.text: German unification brought the German states into a federal empire led by Prussia. The North German Confederation Treaty of 18 August 1866 established an alliance dominated by the Prussian kingdom, followed by a constitution that deepened the union. Southern German states joined in 1871. The ceremonial proclamation of the German Empire on 18 January became its symbolic founding moment, while constitutional changes and the Treaty of Frankfurt completed the legal and diplomatic process that year.

main.title: Yellowstone National Park
main.summary: Yellowstone National Park is a national park of the United States located mainly in the northwest corner of the state of Wyoming, with small portions extending into Montana and Idaho.

cards.heading: Yellowstone National Park
cards.text:
Yellowstone National Park is a national park of the United States located mainly in the northwest corner of the state of Wyoming, with small portions extending into Montana and Idaho. The park is known for its wildlife and its many geothermal features, especially the Old Faithful geyser, one of its most popular. While it represents many types of biomes, subalpine forest is the most abundant. It is part of the South Central Rockies forests ecoregion.

Native Americans have lived in the Yellowstone region for at least 11,000 years. While non-native mountain men visited during the early-to-mid-19th century, organized exploration by non-natives did not begin until the late 1860s. The park was established by the 42nd U.S. Congress through the Yellowstone National Park Protection Act and signed into law by President Ulysses S. Grant on March 1, 1872. Yellowstone was the first national park in the US, and is also widely understood to be the first national park in the world.

main.title: Impressionism
main.summary: The First Impressionist Exhibition in 1874 brought a new approach to light, colour and everyday subjects into public debate.

cards.heading: Impressionism
cards.text:
Impressionism was a 19th-century art movement characterised by visible brush strokes, open composition, emphasis on accurate depiction of light in its changing qualities (often accentuating the effects of the passage of time), ordinary subject matter, unusual visual angles, and inclusion of movement as a crucial element of human perception and experience. Impressionism originated with a group of Paris-based artists whose independent exhibitions brought them to prominence during the 1870s and 1880s.

The Impressionists faced harsh opposition from the conventional art community in France. The name of the style derives from the title of a Claude Monet work, Impression, Sunrise, which provoked the critic Louis Leroy to coin the term in a satirical 1874 review of the First Impressionist Exhibition published in the Parisian newspaper Le Charivari. The development of Impressionism in the visual arts was soon followed by analogous styles in other media that became known as Impressionist music and Impressionist literature.

main.title: Organised ice hockey moves indoors
main.subtitle: A scheduled match at Montreal's Victoria Rink
main.summary: James Creighton organised a public indoor ice-hockey match at Montreal's Victoria Skating Rink on 3 March 1875.

cards.heading: A scheduled match at Montreal's Victoria Rink
cards.text: James George Aylwin Creighton organised an indoor ice-hockey match at Montreal's Victoria Skating Rink on March 3, 1875. Two teams of nine played before spectators with a flattened wooden disc. Creighton's side defeated Charles Torrance's team by two goals to one. A newspaper announcement and subsequent report recorded the event. Bringing named teams, a scheduled contest and an audience into the rink helped establish organised ice hockey as it developed further in Montreal.

main.title: Telephone
main.summary: A telephone, commonly shortened to phone, is a telecommunications device that enables two or more users to conduct a conversation when they are too far apart to be easily heard directly.

cards.heading: Telephone
cards.text:
A telephone, commonly shortened to phone, is a telecommunications device that enables two or more users to conduct a conversation when they are too far apart to be easily heard directly. A telephone converts sound, typically and most efficiently the human voice, into electronic signals that are transmitted via cables and other communication channels to another telephone which reproduces the sound to the receiving user. The term is derived from Ancient Greek: τῆλε, romanized: tēle, lit. 'far' and φωνή (phōnē, voice), together meaning distant voice.

In 1876, Alexander Graham Bell was the first to be granted a United States patent for a device that produced clearly intelligible replication of the human voice at a second device. This instrument was further developed by many others, and became rapidly indispensable in business, government, and in households.

main.title: Phonograph
main.summary: A phonograph, later called a gramophone, and since the 1940s a record player, or more recently a turntable, is a device for the mechanical and analogue reproduction of sound.

cards.heading: Phonograph
cards.text:
A phonograph, later called a gramophone, and since the 1940s a record player, or more recently a turntable, is a device for the mechanical and analogue reproduction of sound.

The sound vibration waveforms are recorded as corresponding physical deviations of a helical or spiral groove engraved, etched, incised, or impressed into the surface of a rotating cylinder or disc, called a record. To recreate the sound, the surface is similarly rotated while a playback stylus traces the groove and is therefore vibrated by it, faintly reproducing the recorded sound. In early acoustic phonographs, the stylus vibrated a diaphragm that produced sound waves coupled to the open air through a flaring horn, or directly to the listener's ears through stethoscope-type earphones.

The phonograph was invented in 1877 by Thomas Edison; Alexander Graham Bell's Volta Laboratory made several improvements in the 1880s and introduced the graphophone, including the use of wax-coated cardboard cylinders and a cutting stylus that moved from side to side in a helical groove around the record.

main.title: Praxinoscope
main.summary: The praxinoscope is an animation device, the successor to the zoetrope.

cards.heading: Praxinoscope
cards.text: The praxinoscope is an animation device, the successor to the zoetrope. It was invented in France in 1877 by Charles-Émile Reynaud. Like the zoetrope, it uses a strip of pictures placed around the inner surface of a spinning cylinder. The praxinoscope improved on the zoetrope by replacing its narrow viewing slits with an inner circle of mirrors, placed so that the reflections of the pictures appeared more or less stationary in position as the wheel turned. Someone looking in the mirrors can, therefore, see a rapid succession of images producing the illusion of motion, with a brighter and less distorted picture than the zoetrope offered.

main.title: The Horse in Motion
main.summary: The Horse in Motion is a series of cabinet cards by Eadweard Muybridge, including six cards that each show a series of six to twelve "automatic electro-photographs" depicting successive phases in the movement of a horse, shot in June 1878.

cards.heading: The Horse in Motion
cards.text:
The Horse in Motion is a series of cabinet cards by Eadweard Muybridge, including six cards that each show a series of six to twelve "automatic electro-photographs" depicting successive phases in the movement of a horse, shot in June 1878. An additional card reprinted the single image of the horse "Occident" trotting at high speed, which had already been published in 1877.

The series became the first example of chronophotography, an early method to photographically record the passing of time, mainly used to document the different phases of locomotion for scientific study. It formed a very influential step in the development of motion pictures. One of the cards (often retitled Sallie Gardner at a Gallop) has even been hailed as "the world's first bit of cinema". Muybridge did project moving images from his photographs with his zoopraxiscope, from 1880 to 1895, but these were painted on discs and his technology was no more advanced than earlier efforts by others (for instance those by Franz von Uchatius in 1853).

main.title: Edison's carbon-filament lamp
main.summary: Thomas Edison successfully tested a carbon-filament incandescent lamp in October 1879.

cards.heading: Edison's carbon-filament lamp
cards.text: Thomas Edison successfully tested a carbon-filament incandescent lamp in October 1879. An electric current heated its filament until it glowed, while a glass bulb protected the material from oxidation. The work formed part of a longer development involving Joseph Swan and other inventors. A practical, inexpensive lamp could bring electric lighting into homes and businesses, then into portable lamps, vehicles and illuminated signs. The familiar bulb joined a simple visible action—light appearing—to the electrical connections and supply needed to sustain it.

main.title: Pearl Street Station begins supplying electricity
main.summary: Pearl Street Station began supplying electricity in Manhattan on 4 September 1882. Built by the Edison Illuminating Company, it initially served 82 customers and around 400 lamps.

cards.heading: Pearl Street Station begins supplying electricity
cards.text:
Pearl Street Station began supplying electricity in Manhattan on 4 September 1882. Built by the Edison Illuminating Company, it initially served 82 customers and around 400 lamps.

Pearl Street Station was Thomas Edison's first commercial power plant in the United States. It was located at 255–257 Pearl Street in the Financial District of Manhattan in New York City, just south of Fulton Street on a site measuring 50 by 100 feet (15 by 30 m). The station was built by the Edison Illuminating Company, under the direction of Francis Upton, hired by Thomas Edison. It had a generation capacity of 600 kW DC.
